title: Arteriogram with Possible Embolization
summary: Arteriography with possible embolization for arterial hemorrhage, including trauma and GI bleeding.
provenance: Imported from procedure orders PDF updated 4.15.26

items: Traumatic arterial bleeding with instability or ongoing transfusion needs.
Persistent/recurrent GI bleeding after failed or infeasible endoscopy.
Active arterial bleeding or symptomatic pseudoaneurysm.
No safe arterial access or catheter route (relative).
Uncorrectable coagulopathy or severe contrast reaction requires individualized planning; weigh against hemorrhage urgency.
No safe embolization target or unacceptable risk to essential organ/bowel perfusion.
A source requiring immediate surgery or another treatment: coordinate the appropriate pathway.
High bleeding risk.
Anticoagulation should already be held for active bleeding; confirm last doses and any reversal given.
Warfarin: hold 5 days and confirm INR <= 1.8.
IV unfractionated heparin: hold 4-6 hours and check aPTT or anti-Xa level.
Enoxaparin: hold 1 dose if prophylactic; hold 2 doses or 24 hours if therapeutic.
DOAC timing is agent-, dose-, and renal-function-specific; use the anticoagulation table.
Clopidogrel and ticagrelor: hold 5 days; prasugrel: hold 7 days.
Aspirin: hold 3-5 days.
Active major hemorrhage: review last doses and reversal with the treating team; elective hold intervals must not delay life-saving source control.
Platelets >50,000/µL.
NPO (if moderate sedation).
Vital signs per routine.
PIV placement (not left arm).
Glucose POC.
Most recent CBC, INR, and CMP.

Arteriogram with Possible Embolization
Bleeding.
Infection.

Persistent or recurrent bleeding requiring repeat embolization or surgery.
left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic branches supply the foregut. The gastroduodenal artery (GDA) usually arises from the common hepatic artery.
inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal/ileal, ileocolic, right colic (variable), and middle colic branches supply distal duodenum through proximal two-thirds of transverse colon.
left colic, sigmoid, and superior rectal branches supply distal transverse/descending colon, sigmoid, and upper rectum.
pancreaticoduodenal arcades connect celiac and SMA territories; marginal colonic arteries connect SMA and IMA. Prior surgery can alter these routes.
map replaced/accessory hepatic arteries. Trauma targets may involve splenic, renal, pelvic/internal iliac, or chest-wall branches rather than GI vessels.
femoral puncture should permit compression over the femoral head; radial access requires an appropriate artery and a patent route to the target.
localize bleeding and review variants/collaterals.
use ultrasound-guided femoral or radial access; place the sheath.
perform angiography to identify extravasation or pseudoaneurysm.
advance the microcatheter; confirm the target and branches to preserve.
coils, gelatin, particles, or liquid agent according to target and flow.
watch for reflux, catheter movement, and nontarget filling.
confirm hemostasis, assess collateral filling, and preserve uninvolved perfusion.
obtain access hemostasis and document the treatment and handoff.

use ultrasound to mark the CFA bifurcation into SFA/profunda and avoid anterior-wall plaque. Use a radiopaque marker and AP fluoroscopy to locate the femoral head. The arteriotomy should overlie the head, above the bifurcation and below the inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle). Skin entry is caudal to the intended arterial puncture; the crease alone is unreliable.

prep, drape, and infiltrate lidocaine. Under ultrasound, enter the anterior wall with a 21G needle. Advance the 0.018-inch microwire into the iliac artery under fluoroscopy; stop for resistance or a subintimal course.

advance the 4 Fr transitional introducer, remove its inner dilator/microwire, and insert a 0.035-inch Bentson. Exchange the introducer for a 5 Fr arterial sheath over the wire; aspirate and flush the sidearm.

perform sidearm angiography at about 30 degrees ipsilateral oblique: RAO for right CFA, LAO for left. Gently retract the sheath externally enough to display entry without dislodging it. Confirm CFA entry over the head, below the ligament and above bifurcation; check for extravasation, dissection, stenosis, or pseudoaneurysm.

use CTA/endoscopy to choose celiac, SMA, or IMA rather than searching blindly. Advance the Bentson into the upper abdominal aorta under fluoroscopy. Typical diagnostic catheters: 5 Fr Cobra C2, Simmons 1/2, or SOS Omni; choose the curve for the ostium.

celiac usually arises near T12-L1; SMA near L1. Withdraw the wire, connect a contrast syringe, and gently withdraw/rotate the catheter with small hand puffs until the origin engages. Confirm free flow and no wedging before DSA.

prime and de-air injector tubing; confirm catheter rating and test injection. SMA example: 5 mL/s, 25 mL total (5 seconds). Celiac commonly 4-6 mL/s, 12-15 mL total; use the table below. Review through the delayed phase for extravasation, pseudoaneurysm, or collateral filling.

use a 0.035-inch angled Glidewire through the 5 Fr catheter for larger branches; advance the catheter over the wire, never against resistance. Identify the source and branches to preserve before advancing distally.

example: Progreat 2.4 Fr, 110/130 cm, with a 0.016-inch Fathom-16 wire (often 180 cm). Progreat 2.4 accepts wires up to 0.018 inch. Flush/de-air both devices, wet the hydrophilic wire, and use a saline-filled hemostatic valve. Advance the microcatheter through the base catheter with the microwire leading under fluoroscopy.

advance to the culprit branch while preserving uninvolved supply. Withdraw the microwire for a gentle test injection and DSA. Do not default to 3 mL/s through a 2.4 Fr Progreat: its flow depends on length, contrast, and pressure limits. Reduce injection for small or wedged branches; never force a high-pressure run.

choose coils, gelatin sponge, liquid embolic/glue, or a plug for target, flow, and coagulation status. For a GDA/pseudoaneurysm with back-door flow, assess distal and proximal feeders; distal-then-proximal exclusion may be needed. Do not occlude the GDA before checking whether it supplies the liver via SMA collaterals in celiac stenosis.

measure the landing-zone lumen on calibrated angiography. For coils that require oversizing, about 20% is a common reference: a 5 mm vessel suggests a 6 mm coil. Coil design changes sizing; follow the selected coil instructions. Confirm microcatheter inner-diameter/delivery compatibility and a stable landing zone. Deploy under fluoroscopy; stop for kickback or migration.

for small-bowel/colonic bleeding, embolize the shortest feasible culprit territory, ideally a superselected bleeding vasa recta. Preserve the marginal artery and adjacent branches. The splenic flexure/middle-colic-left-colic watershed can have weak collaterals; distal to the middle colic is not a universal boundary. Avoid broad or multibranch embolization.

repeat DSA from the parent vessel to confirm hemostasis and preserved uninvolved flow. After celiac/GDA treatment, obtain an SMA run when pancreaticoduodenal back-door filling is relevant; check other feeders according to the bleeding territory. Persistent instability with a negative run may reflect intermittent bleeding, not technical success.

remove catheters over a wire and achieve access hemostasis by the chosen closure device or manual compression. Document treated branches/embolics, residual collateral flow, and distal pulses; use the existing Access care orders.

blocks.caption: Contrast injection settings
blocks.note: Adult iodinated-contrast reference only. Confirm tip position, test injection, flow, catheter/pressure limits, and attending settings; never power inject a wedged catheter. Portal 7/21 is a local example pending confirmation.

items: bleeding may be intermittent or obscured by vasospasm; correlate CTA/endoscopy and discuss a targeted plan rather than indiscriminate embolization.
recheck the tip before delivery; stop injection if reflux or nontarget filling appears.
keep treatment selective, preserve collaterals, and account for prior surgery, radiation, or poor baseline perfusion.
collaterals can refill the lesion; assess relevant inflow/outflow, especially GDA/pancreaticoduodenal pathways.
avoid forceful wire advancement, wedged injections, and unnecessary manipulation; reassess new dissection or extravasation.
check access-site swelling and distal perfusion; persistent instability needs prompt reassessment even after an angiographic endpoint.

blocks.title: Routine orders
items: Diet - Outpatient: order regular diet. Inpatient: notify primary team diet is okay.
Tylenol 650 mg PRN.
Vital signs every 15 minutes x 4, then every 30 minutes x 2, then every 1 hour x 4, then every 4 hours; edit to match bedrest.
Bedrest 2 hours with closure device; 6 hours with manual compression.
Monitor color of access site.

1: Remove radial artery compression device within 2 hours post procedure.

blocks.title: Anticoagulation to resume
items: Warfarin: 24 hours.
IV unfractionated heparin: 6-8 hours.
Enoxaparin: 12 hours.
DOACs: Typically 24 hours; confirm agent and renal function.
Clopidogrel: 75 mg dose - 6 hours; 300-600 mg loading dose - 24 hours.
Aspirin: 24 hours.
Restart after hemostasis is confirmed; individualize timing for procedure-specific or patient-specific exceptions.

items: Discharge order with medication reconciliation - 2-6 hours.
